newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Rifkind nudges Israelis, Palestinians on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Rifkind nudges Israelis, Palestinians on Hebron.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind tried during a one-day Middle East mission on Sunday to nudge Israeli and Palestinian peacemakers closer to an accord on the sticking point of Hebron.

"There is a real prospect for agreement on Hebron over the near future but that will require both sides to address these matters in an inspired way that recognises the great prizes to be won," Rifkind told reporters.
He spoke during a joint news conference with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy before heading to Hebron, an Israeli-occupied West Bank city long overdue to be handed over to Palestinian self-rule.

Rifkind's Hebron visit, sandwiched between talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, President Ezer Weizman and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, was cleared with his Israeli hosts, British officials said.

Britain sees the delayed redeployment of troops from Hebron, first postponed after a wave of Moslem militant suicide bombings and put on hold again after Netanyahu's election in May, as one of the key reasons for the build-up of Palestinian frustration at the slow progress towards peace.

But British diplomats steadfastly denied Rifkind would try to rival French President Jacques Chirac, who during a visit last week publicly turned on Israeli security men and accused them of provocation during a visit to Jerusalem's Old City and was given a hero's welcome by Palestinians.

Although careful to avoid criticising Chirac's visit, Rifkind emphasised: "We are even-handed". He said Israel and the Palestinians should work out their own disputes and the role of the international community was to assist.
Privately, London -- which wants Europe to complement rather than try to supplant the mediation efforts of the United States -- is wary of Chirac's diplomatic intentions.
Officials stressed Rifkind was determined to avoid "megaphone diplomacy" or "grandstanding" -- a word used by British newspaper commentators to describe Chirac's behaviour.

Rifkind is determined to keep up pressure for a deal, even though there is a risk his visit to Hebron will inflame hardline Jewish settlers in the West Bank. British diplomats said they expected the visit to go smoothly although they were ready to change plans if there was any hint of disturbances.
The city, where 400 Jews live in the heart of 100,000 Arabs, is a flashpoint of violence.

Levy welcomed Rifkind's arrival in the region, suggesting the British minister's status with Israel and its Arab neighbours might be able to break a freeze in negotiations with Israel's arch-foe Syria.

Talks with Syria have been stuck on the future of the Golan Heights, which Damascus wants back. Israel captured the strategic plateau in the 1967 Middle East war and Netanyahu opposes giving any of it back.
Levy appealed to Damascus to negotiate. Rifkind said "painful private diplomacy" was required to restore confidence and trust between Israel and Syria.
Rifkind flew into Israel from Vietnam after accompanying Queen Elizabeth on a vist to Thailand. He leaves on Monday for Abu Dhabi.
